sourceDocuments.text: At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most toward the Sun, and the Southern Hemisphere away; the relation reverses in December. The June solstice gives the longest daylight of the year at ordinary northern midlatitudes and the shortest at southern midlatitudes. Seasons arise primarily from axial tilt, not Earth-Sun distance.

text:
I'll analyze each item carefully.

---

**Item 0:**

The stem establishes Oslo's sunrise at 3:54 AM local time on the June solstice, then asks about Cape Town's sunrise.

Evaluating the correct candidate: "Sunrise occurs later than 6:00 AM and later than on the December solstice."

- At 34°S on the June solstice, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun → winter → short days → sunrise after 6:00 AM local solar time. ✓
- On the December solstice, 34°S is in summer → sunrise is earlier than on the June solstice. ✓

Both conditions are well-supported by solar geometry. The other choices are clearly refuted. Exactly one valid answer. The question requires interpreting hemispheric tilt effects and comparing two dates — difficulty 3 is appropriate.

---

**Item 1:**

The stem asks on which *pair of dates* will both locations (40°N and 40°S) experience approximately equal daylight hours.

The question requires "both locations experience approximately equal daylight hours" — this must hold on both dates in the pair.

- "March equinox and September equinox": At both equinoxes, all latitudes get ~12 hours of daylight. Both locations equal on both dates. ✓
- The other pairs each include a solstice, where the two hemispheres have opposite extremes (unequal). ✗

Exactly one valid answer. Difficulty 3 is appropriate — requires understanding that equinoxes equalize daylight across hemispheres while solstices do the opposite.

choices.reason: At 34°S on the June solstice, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, giving shorter days and later sunrises than 6:00 AM. Tilt effects do not 'cancel' at this latitude; they produce winter conditions in the Southern Hemisphere.

choices.choice: Sunrise timing cannot be determined without knowing Cape Town's longitude.
choices.reason: Longitude affects the exact clock time only within a time zone, but the question asks about local solar time behavior. The general pattern—that Cape Town has a late sunrise on the June solstice due to Southern Hemisphere winter—is determinable from latitude and date alone.

choices.choice: Sunrise occurs later than 6:00 AM and later than on the December solstice.
choices.reason: On the June solstice, 34°S is in mid-winter: days are shortest, so sunrise is after 6:00 AM local solar time. On the December solstice (Southern Hemisphere summer), sunrise is earlier. Both conditions in this choice are consistent with established solar geometry.

choices.choice: Sunrise occurs earlier than 3:54 AM, matching Oslo's early sunrise.
choices.reason: Oslo's extremely early sunrise (3:54 AM) results from its high northern latitude (59°N) experiencing near-maximum summer daylight. Cape Town at 34°S is in winter on the June solstice and has a late sunrise, not an early one comparable to Oslo's.

On the June solstice, 40°N has long days (~15 h) and 40°S has short days (~9 h)—very unequal. On the March equinox both have ~12 h, so only one of the two dates gives equal daylight; the pair as a whole does not satisfy 'both locations experience approximately equal daylight hours' on both dates.
On the December solstice, 40°S has long days and 40°N has short days—unequal. On the September equinox both have ~12 h. Again only one date in the pair gives equal daylight, not both dates.

At both equinoxes, all latitudes experience approximately 12 hours of daylight regardless of hemisphere. So on both the March and September equinoxes, 40°N and 40°S each have ~12 h of daylight—equal on both dates.

On the June solstice, 40°N has ~15 h and 40°S has ~9 h (unequal). On the December solstice the situation reverses (40°S ~15 h, 40°N ~9 h)—still unequal on each date, even though the two locations swap roles.
